To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ERM is still effective in estimating the regression coefficient vector even when the noise and input variables are dependent and heavy-talled.

(a) the empirical minimizer of a strictly stationary exponentially $\alpha$-mixing process is a good estimator of the population minimizer with high probability and (b) this result holds even for the heavy-tailed case.

(i) ERM can still learn the optimal model with dependent heavy-tailed data, (ii) the rate of convergence of the excess risk is the same as that of the independent and identically distribution case (up to log factors), and (iii) this rate is optimal in a minimax sense.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How can we learn a model from data that is both dependent and heavy tailed?
the following question: How does the data-generating process affect the statistical learning of ERM with polynomially heavy-tail distributions?
the following questions: 1) How does the ERM perform when the data are dependent?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ERM algorithm is able to learn a class of linear models from dependent and heavy-tail data.
the ERM algorithm can be used for dependent data as well, provided that the data is not too dependent.
the ERM with dependent data and heavy-tailed distributions can still be analyzed and the results are not as bad as one might expect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, under the assumption that data-generating processes satisfy a certain form of exponential mixing and the loss function is polynomially bounded, we show that the ERM is still a consistent and efficient estimator.
, in a nonparametric regression setting with dependent and heavy tailed observations, ERM can be used to achieve the optimal rate of convergence in the minimax sense.

we provide a theoretical foundation for learning with dependent data that is as general as the existing theory for learning with independent heavy-tailed data, which is a major step towards closing the gap between the two fields.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ERM is robust with respect to the heavy-tailed data and the dependency structure.
, under a suitable dependence structure, heavy-tailedness does not hinder learning.
, in the dependent setting, the rate of convergence of the ERM estimator can be slower than the rate of convergence in the independent setting.
